extracted.intended_audience: scholars, critics, and educated readers evaluating scientific, philosophical, or sociological arguments (esp. on evolution and scientific terminology)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for critiquing scientific/philosophical claims and formulas (e.g., definitions of force, the formula of Evolution), stressing careful use of language, attention to scope and conditions, and appropriate disciplinary familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult latest editions / authoritative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A conscientious critic usually consults the latest edition of the work he criticizes, so that the author may have the benefit of any corrections or alterations he has made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base criticism on outdated text or early editions; check for revisions/errata before judging an author's statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent definition and reconciliation of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author (e.g., Professor Tait) uses multiple definitions of a term (for example, 'force' as that which changes the state of a body versus 'force' as the rate at which an agent does work), a critic must note the apparent contradiction and seek how the statements are to be reconciled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare differing formulations, identify whether they refer to same concept or different aspects (agent vs rate), and avoid accepting inconsistent usages without resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid category errors (relations vs agents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat relations (rates, ratios) as if they were agents capable of producing phenomena — e.g., a 'rate' is a relation, not an entity that 'changes the state of a body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with ontological categories in critique; challenge confusions where a relation is implicitly reified into a causal agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize necessity of abstract language for universal formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: A formula expressing all orders of changes (astronomic, geologic, biologic, psychologic, sociologic) could not possibly be framed in any other than words of the highest abstractness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss apparently 'vague' technical terms just because they lack vivid, concrete images; abstract words often are necessary to express wide generalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate unfamiliarity with meaninglessness
rubrics_metrics.description: If abstract or highly general words are unintelligible to the uninitiated, this does not prove them meaningless; lack of corresponding images in the hearer can make terms seem vague or empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach or exemplify the abstract idea with concrete instances rather than assuming the term is empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of crude 'translation' traps
rubrics_metrics.description: Transforming technical words into awkward literal Saxon equivalents (e.g., 'homogeneity' → 'all-alikeness', 'integrations' → 'sticktogetherations') can produce nonsense and thereby misrepresent the original meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should not rely on mock translations to show a theory's emptiness; preserve the technical nuance rather than caricaturing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish intrinsic absurdity from extrinsic absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a great difference between disclosing absurdities contained in a thing and piling absurdities upon it; some minds cannot distinguish intrinsic from extrinsic absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When showing that a claim is absurd, ensure the absurdity is inherent to the claim, not an artifact introduced by the critic's parody or bad analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain disciplinary breadth — analytical and synthetical habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical training (abstract and mathematical sciences) and synthetical training (concrete sciences) cultivate different powers; exclusive familiarity with one group leaves defects of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should acquire or consult across scientific groups: analytical skill alone may miss traits of general transformations, while concrete familiarity without abstract training may miss general principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep simultaneously in view all associated traits of a formula
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticizing a complex generalization (e.g., the formula of Evolution), do not dissociate the several traits that together constitute it; many objections fail if the traits are considered together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the full, qualified statement (including secondary qualifications) before isolating aspects for criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish levels/scopes of analysis (individual vs aggregate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between processes as they apply to single systems (e.g., one language) and to aggregates (e.g., languages as a group); conflating these leads to mistaken objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether an alleged counterexample refers to the same level (individual vs aggregate) that the generalization addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate integration (coherence) from homogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration (the change from incoherent to coherent — 'integration of matter and concomitant dissipation of motion') is the primary evolutionary process and is not the same as increase of homogeneity; integration often leads to greater internal heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting social, economic, or biological changes, treat integration/coherence separately from sameness; look for increased complexity and differentiation within integrated wholes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret apparent unifying trends correctly (supplanting vs assimilation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The disappearance of dialects or varieties by supplanting does not constitute a tendency of remaining items to become alike; extinction of varieties is not the same as progression towards homogeneity among surviving varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether a unifying process is elimination of diversity or actual assimilation causing internal homogenization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for conditions and contingency
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of Evolution is not necessary but depends on conditions; prevalence of Evolution in the universe is consequent on the prevalence of these conditions, and dissolution can occur where they fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating broad generalizations as inevitable laws independent of boundary conditions; consider where conditions change and reverse processes may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect transitional mixtures during metamorphoses
rubrics_metrics.description: During transitions (dissolution of one type and evolution of another) there will be mixtures of structures causing apparent confusion or anomalies; temporary blurring is to be expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer that temporary anomalies disprove the general trend; interpret such jumbling as part of metamorphosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete empirical familiarity when judging abstract claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics unfamiliar with complex concrete processes (e.g., general transformations shown by the concrete sciences) are liable to form shadowy thoughts when confronted with abstract formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground abstract generalizations in empirical examples from concrete sciences when defending or critiquing them; seek input from concrete-domain expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish primary and secondary traits in a generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Some traits (e.g., integration/coherence) are primary, while others (e.g., change from homogeneity to heterogeneity) are secondary and accompany the primary trait when conditions allow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating objections, determine which traits are core to the generalization and which are contingent or derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dismissing generalizations because they are 'blank forms'
rubrics_metrics.description: A formula that seems like a 'blank form for a universe' may still correctly express universal relations; lack of immediate vividness does not negate explanatory power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the formula captures essential relations across domains rather than rejecting it for lacking concrete, picturesque language.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using analogies across domains, check applicability of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies (e.g., laws of molar and molecular motion applying across physical, biological, social phenomena) should be used carefully; the presence of common traits supports generalization but requires evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test analogical claims against domain-specific evidence; be cautious but open to cross-domain applicability when justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on rhetorical mockery to refute technical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridiculing technical terminology by substituting absurd homely paraphrases (to 'dissipate' glamour) is not a valid mode of refutation if it misrepresents the intended technical import.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with technical content on its own terms; if a term seems obscure, ask for clarification or examples rather than caricature.
